newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - France, Germany pledge to meet EMU deficit goals.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - France, Germany pledge to meet EMU deficit goals.

text.p: France and Germany on Tuesday reiterated their determination to bring their budget deficits below three percent of GDP next year, in an austerity drive which may leave other European countries trailing.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel told a news conference after a meeting with his French counterpart and central bankers that the two countries would stick to their aims.
"We agreed that we aimed to take our budget deficits below three percent," he said.

French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis, who presents France's 1997 budget on Wednesday morning, declined to confirm that France planned to announce a target for the deficit/GDP ratio actually below three percent.
"The sum of the public borrowing requirements will be contained within the three percent limit," he told reporters.
If France and Germany actually meet their targets, it will be harder for countries with bigger budget deficits to join monetary union when it is first launched in 1999.
Germany has pledged to bring its 1997 budget deficit down to 2.5 percent of GDP.

Belief earlier this year that France and maybe even Germany would overshoot the three percent limit in 1997 had raised hopes in peripheral mediterranean states -- particularly Spain -- of making the first wave of monetary union if deficits were reduced to below four percent of GDP.
The Maastricht treaty allows some leeway on deficits, taking account of a downward trend toward three percent.

France's budget will include a mix of spending reductions and tax cuts which the government hopes will bolster investor confidence, encourage consumer spending and possibly pave the way for lower interest rates.
Economists said the Bank of France may reward the government's fiscal rectitude with a cut in its key intervention rate as early as Thursday.
Bank of France Governor Jean-Claude Trichet, however, when asked whether interest rates will be cut after the budget, said rates in France were already at historic lows.
"You have to consider that already the Bank of France and the money markets on the the other hand have delivered very low market rates," he said.
